title: Pressure, Particles and Diffusion
summary: How to calculate pressure, how particles cause pressure in gases and liquids, and how diffusion mixes gases and liquids — with worked examples, common mistakes and a Checkpoint-style quiz.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Explain that pressure is caused by a force acting on an area, and calculate it with pressure = force ÷ area. (8Pf.05)
Use the particle model to explain pressure in gases and liquids (no calculations needed). (8Pf.06)
Describe diffusion in gases and liquids as the mixing of substances caused by the movement of their particles. (8Pf.07)

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: pressure
الضغط — the force acting on each unit of area
area
المساحة — the size of a surface, in m² or cm²
pascal (Pa)
باسكال — the unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m²
particle
جسيم — a tiny piece of matter (atom or molecule)
collision
تصادم — when a particle hits another particle or a wall
gas pressure
ضغط الغاز — caused by gas particles hitting the walls of their container
depth
العمق — how far below the surface
compress
يضغط / ينضغط — squash into a smaller volume
diffusion
الانتشار — particles mixing and spreading out because they move randomly
concentration
التركيز — how many particles of a substance are in a space
random
عشوائي — in any direction, with no pattern

blocks.text: 2. What is pressure?

Press your palm on a balloon and nothing happens; press a pin on it with the same force and it bursts. The force is the same — what changes is the **area** it acts on. **Pressure** tells us how concentrated a force is: how much force acts on each square metre (or square centimetre) of surface.

blocks.title: The formula
blocks.text: **pressure = force ÷ area**   (p = F ÷ A). Force in newtons (N), area in m² → pressure in **N/m²**, also called **pascals (Pa)**. Area in cm² → pressure in **N/cm²**.

blocks.text: **Rearranging.** Use a formula triangle with F on top and p × A underneath: **force = pressure × area** and **area = force ÷ pressure**.

blocks.title: Areas and units
blocks.text: Areas are in **square** units. To change m² to cm² multiply by **10 000** (1 m = 100 cm, so 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm²). So 1 N/cm² = 10 000 N/m² = 10 000 Pa. Use the area of the surface **touching** the ground — for a cuboid, length × width of the face it rests on, never the volume.
3. Pressure in gases: the particle model

In a gas the particles are far apart and move **quickly and randomly** in all directions. They keep **colliding** with the walls of their container. Each collision gives the wall a tiny push (a force). Billions of collisions every second, spread over the area of the wall, cause **gas pressure**. Gas pressure pushes **in all directions** — that is why a balloon is round.

blocks.caption: Gas pressure is caused by particles colliding with the walls of the container.

rows: **more gas** in the same container (pumping up a tyre)
more particles → more collisions with the walls each second
particles move faster → they hit the walls more often and harder
**smaller volume** (pushing in a syringe with the end blocked)
particles have less space → they hit the walls more often
fewer air particles above you and around you

blocks.text: Gases can be **compressed** (squashed) because there are big spaces between the particles. You can push in the plunger of a blocked syringe full of air, but not one full of water.
4. Pressure in liquids

In a liquid the particles are **touching** but can move past each other. They also collide with the walls of the container and with any object in the liquid, so liquids exert pressure too. Three facts to learn:

items: **Pressure increases with depth.** The deeper you go, the more liquid there is above pushing down. This is why a dam is built much thicker at the bottom, why divers' ears hurt in deep water, and why water spurts hardest from the lowest hole in a tank.
**Liquid pressure acts in all directions** — down, up and sideways — because the particles move in all directions.
**Liquids cannot be compressed** (almost), because the particles are already touching. So a push on one part of a liquid is passed on through the liquid. Car brakes and hydraulic lifts use this idea.

blocks.caption: Water spurts out hardest from the deepest hole (C), because the pressure is greatest at the greatest depth.

blocks.title: الضغط
items: الضغط = القوة ÷ المساحة، ووحدته باسكال (Pa) = نيوتن/متر² أو نيوتن/سم².
نفس القوة على مساحة صغيرة ← ضغط كبير (السكينة الحادة، المسمار). على مساحة كبيرة ← ضغط صغير (أحذية الجليد، رجل الجمل).
ضغط الغاز سببه تصادم جزيئات الغاز مع جدران الإناء. وفي السوائل الضغط بيزيد كل ما ننزل لتحت (العمق يزيد)، وبيأثر في كل الاتجاهات.

blocks.text: 5. Diffusion

Spray perfume in one corner of a room and soon people on the other side can smell it, even though nobody has moved the air. This spreading is called **diffusion**. It happens because particles of gases and liquids are **always moving randomly**. As they move and bump into each other, the particles of the two substances **intermingle (mix)**. Overall, particles spread from where there are **many** of them (high concentration) to where there are **few** (low concentration), until they are **evenly mixed**.

blocks.caption: Diffusion of two gases. No stirring is needed: random movement of the particles mixes them evenly.

items: **Gases** diffuse quickly: the particles move fast and there is lots of space between them (smells, perfume, a gas leak).

**Liquids** diffuse slowly: the particles are touching and keep bumping into each other (a drop of ink or food colouring in water, a tea bag in a cup, a purple potassium permanganate crystal in water).
**Solids** do not diffuse in everyday life: the particles only vibrate in fixed positions.
**Higher temperature → faster diffusion**, because the particles move faster.
Lighter particles move faster than heavier ones at the same temperature, so they diffuse faster.
Even when the mixing is complete, the particles **keep moving** — the mixture just stays evenly mixed.
Diffusion matters in living things: oxygen diffuses from the air in the lungs into the blood, and carbon dioxide diffuses the other way.

blocks.text: **Investigating diffusion (working scientifically).** Put one drop of food colouring into beakers of water at 20 °C, 40 °C and 60 °C, and time how long the water takes to become evenly coloured. **Independent variable:** temperature. **Dependent variable:** time to become evenly coloured. **Control variables:** volume of water, size of the drop, same colouring, no stirring, same size of beaker. **Prediction:** the hotter the water, the shorter the time, because the particles move faster. **Risk:** hot water can scald — handle the beakers carefully.

blocks.title: الانتشار
items: الانتشار = اختلاط المواد بسبب حركة جزيئاتها العشوائية، من المكان اللي فيه جزيئات كتير (تركيز عالي) للمكان اللي فيه جزيئات قليلة — من غير تقليب.
بيحصل أسرع في الغازات من السوائل (الجزيئات أسرع والمسافات بينها أكبر)، وبيكون أسرع لما الحرارة تزيد.
مثال: ريحة البرفان بتوصل لآخر الأوضة، ونقطة الحبر بتلوّن المية كلها.

blocks.text: 6. Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — A box has a weight of 600 N. The area of its base is 1.5 m². Calculate the pressure it exerts on the floor. [2]

items: pressure = force ÷ area

blocks.text: **Worked example 2** — Mona weighs 480 N. Each of her shoes has an area of 160 cm² touching the floor. (a) Calculate the pressure when she stands on both feet. [2] (b) What happens to the pressure when she stands on one foot? [1]

items: (a) Area of two shoes = 2 × 160 = 320 cm². Pressure = 480 ÷ 320 = **1.5 N/cm²**.
(b) The area halves (160 cm²), so the pressure **doubles**: 480 ÷ 160 = **3 N/cm²**.
**Common mistake:** in (a), using the area of only one shoe.

blocks.text: **Worked example 3** — A tractor has a weight of 60 000 N. To stop it sinking into a muddy field, the pressure on the ground must be no more than 40 000 Pa. What is the smallest total area its tyres must have? [2]

items: Rearrange: area = force ÷ pressure (1)
This is why tractors have very wide tyres.

blocks.text: **Worked example 4** — A sealed can of air is heated. Explain why the pressure inside the can increases. [3]

items: When the air is heated, its particles **move faster** (1).
They **collide with the walls of the can more often** (1)…
…and **with more force** each time, so the pressure increases (1).
**Common mistake:** "the particles expand" or "the particles get bigger". Particles never change size — they move faster.

blocks.text: **Worked example 5** — A drop of blue ink is added to a glass of water. Without stirring, the whole glass slowly turns pale blue. (a) Name this process. [1] (b) Explain why it would happen faster in hot water. [1]

items: (a) **Diffusion.**
(b) In hot water the particles **move faster**, so they mix (intermingle) more quickly.

blocks.text: **Worked example 6** — Explain why a dam is built thicker at the bottom than at the top. [2]

items: Water pressure **increases with depth** (1)…
…so the water pushes hardest on the bottom of the dam, and the bottom must be strongest / thickest to withstand the greater force (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Dividing area by force. Pressure = **force ÷ area**.
Using a volume instead of an area, or forgetting that area is in **square** units (m² or cm²).
Forgetting to add the areas when someone stands on two feet, or a vehicle has four tyres.
Saying that particles "expand", "get bigger" or "get excited" when heated. They **move faster**.
Saying gas pressure is caused by particles "pushing each other". It is caused by particles **colliding with the walls**.
Thinking liquid pressure only pushes down. It acts in **all directions**.
Describing diffusion as "particles moving from high to low" with no mention of **random movement** or mixing — and saying it needs stirring. Diffusion happens **without** stirring.
Saying solids diffuse like liquids. In solids the particles only vibrate.

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Calculate pressure** (often 3 marks): find the area (add feet or tyres), divide the weight by the area, give the unit (Pa, N/m² or N/cm²).
**Rearrange** to find a force or an area.
**Explain an everyday design** using area and pressure: knives, snowshoes, drawing pins, tractor tyres, bag straps.
**Explain gas pressure** with particles: moving randomly, colliding with walls, more collisions → more pressure.
**Explain changes**: pumping in more air, heating a sealed container, squashing a syringe.
**Liquids**: pressure increases with depth (dams, divers, holes in a tank).
**Diffusion**: name it, describe what you would see, explain with random particle movement, and say how temperature affects the rate.

blocks.title: Pressure, particles and diffusion — practice
blocks.intro: Answer every part. Type short answers in the box; for longer answers write yours on paper first, then mark it with the mark scheme.

questions.q: Which is a unit of pressure?
c: N
N/m²
N m
m/s
questions.e: Pressure = force ÷ area, so its unit is **newtons per square metre (N/m²)**, also called the **pascal (Pa)**. N/cm² is also used. N is the unit of force, N m is the unit of a moment and m/s is the unit of speed.

questions.q: A crate with a weight of 900 N rests on a floor. The area of its base is 3 m². Calculate the pressure it exerts on the floor.
questions.e: pressure = force ÷ area = 900 ÷ 3 = **300 Pa** (300 N/m²). The force here is the crate's weight. (1 mark for the working, 1 mark for the answer with unit.)

questions.q: A girl has a weight of 500 N. She stands on both feet. The total area of her two shoe soles touching the ground is 250 cm². Calculate the pressure on the ground in N/cm².
questions.e: pressure = force ÷ area = 500 ÷ 250 = **2 N/cm²**. If she stood on one foot, the area would halve and the pressure would double to 4 N/cm².

questions.q: A car tyre presses on the road with a pressure of 50 000 Pa. The area of the tyre touching the road is 0.02 m². Calculate the force of the tyre on the road.
questions.e: Rearrange: force = pressure × area = 50 000 × 0.02 = **1000 N**. Common mistake: dividing (50 000 ÷ 0.02 = 2 500 000) — cover F in the triangle: P and A are side by side, so multiply.

questions.q: Why does a sharp knife cut bread more easily than a blunt knife?
c: The sharp knife is heavier.
The sharp knife has a larger area of blade touching the bread.
The sharp blade has a smaller area, so the same force gives a bigger pressure.
The sharp knife needs less force because it has no friction.
questions.e: A sharp edge has a very **small area**. Pressure = force ÷ area, so the same force over a smaller area gives a **much bigger pressure**, which cuts the bread. A blunt knife has a larger area, so the pressure is lower.

questions.q: A balloon is filled with air. Use the particle model to explain how the air inside causes a pressure on the inside of the balloon. [2]
questions.ms: 1 mark: air/gas particles are moving (quickly, randomly, in all directions) and collide with / hit the inside wall of the balloon. 1 mark: each collision exerts a (small) force on the wall; the force of many collisions on the area of the wall causes the pressure / pressure = force of collisions per unit area. Do not accept 'the particles expand' or 'the particles push because they get bigger'.
questions.e: The air particles are **moving quickly in all directions**. They keep **colliding with the inside surface** of the balloon. Each collision **pushes on the wall** with a small force. Billions of collisions every second, spread over the area of the wall, produce the **pressure** that keeps the balloon blown up.

questions.q: Hamza pumps more air into a bicycle tyre. The temperature stays the same. Why does the pressure in the tyre increase?
c: There are more particles, so they hit the walls of the tyre more often.
The particles get bigger, so they push harder on the walls.
The particles move more slowly, so they press on the walls for longer.
The particles stop moving and fill up the tyre.
questions.e: Adding air adds **more particles** to the same space, so there are **more collisions with the walls every second**, and the pressure increases. Particles never get bigger, and at the same temperature they move at the same speeds.

questions.p:
Question 8
A tank of water stands on a stand. It has three small holes, A, B and C, all the same size.

questions.q: From which hole does the water come out with the greatest force? Write A, B or C.
questions.e: **C**. Pressure in a liquid **increases with depth**, because there is more water above pushing down. Hole C is the deepest, so the pressure there is greatest and the water is pushed out hardest (and lands furthest away).

questions.q:
Write the missing word.
The smell of cooking spreads through a house because particles move and mix by ________.
questions.e: **Diffusion** — the particles of the smell move randomly and mix (intermingle) with the air particles, spreading from where there are many of them (the kitchen) to where there are few.

questions.q: Why does diffusion happen faster in gases than in liquids?
c: Gas particles are bigger than liquid particles.
Gas particles are joined together in a pattern.
Liquid particles do not move at all.
Gas particles move faster and have much more space between them.
questions.e: In a gas the particles are **far apart** and move **quickly**, so they spread out fast. In a liquid the particles are touching and keep bumping into each other, so they mix more slowly. Liquid particles do move — that is why diffusion happens in liquids at all.

questions.q:
A purple crystal of potassium permanganate is placed carefully at the bottom of a beaker of water. The water is **not** stirred.
Describe what you would see over the next few hours, and explain it using ideas about particles. [3]
questions.ms: 1 mark: the purple colour spreads through the water / the water slowly turns purple. 1 mark: until all the water is the same (paler) purple colour / evenly coloured. 1 mark: particles of potassium permanganate and water move randomly / mix by diffusion / move from where there are many purple particles to where there are few. Do not accept 'the crystal melts'. Accept 'the crystal dissolves' as part of the description.
questions.e: **What you see:** the crystal dissolves and a purple colour slowly spreads upwards and outwards through the water, until after some hours **all the water is the same pale purple colour**. **Explanation:** the particles of potassium permanganate and the water particles are **always moving randomly**. They **intermingle (mix)**, so there is an overall movement of purple particles from where there are many (near the crystal) to where there are few. This is **diffusion**. No stirring is needed because the particles move on their own.

questions.p:
Question 12
Cotton wool soaked in ammonia solution is put in one end of a long glass tube, and cotton wool soaked in hydrochloric acid in the other end, at the same time. Ammonia gas and hydrogen chloride gas diffuse along the tube. Where they meet, they react and make a white ring of solid ammonium chloride.

questions.q: The white ring forms nearer the hydrochloric acid end. What does this tell you?
c: Hydrogen chloride particles move faster than ammonia particles.
Both gases move at the same speed.
Ammonia particles move faster than hydrogen chloride particles, so they travel further in the same time.
Ammonia particles are heavier than hydrogen chloride particles.
questions.e: In the same time, the ammonia particles travelled **further** (more than half the tube) than the hydrogen chloride particles, so ammonia **diffuses faster**. This is because ammonia particles are **lighter** (smaller mass), so they move faster at the same temperature.

questions.q:
A brick measures 20 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm and has a weight of 30 N. It can rest on any of its faces.
Calculate the **greatest** pressure the brick can exert on the ground, in N/cm². Show your working.
questions.e: The greatest pressure comes from the **smallest area** (1). Face areas: 20 × 10 = 200 cm², 20 × 5 = 100 cm², 10 × 5 = **50 cm²** (smallest) (1). Pressure = 30 ÷ 50 = **0.6 N/cm²** (1). Common mistake: using the volume (20 × 10 × 5 = 1000) instead of an area.

questions.q:
A woman has a weight of 600 N. For a moment, all her weight rests on the heel of one shoe, with an area of 1 cm². In flat shoes, her weight is spread over an area of 150 cm².
How many times greater is the pressure under the heel than under the flat shoes?
questions.e: Heel: 600 ÷ 1 = **600 N/cm²**. Flat shoes: 600 ÷ 150 = **4 N/cm²**. 600 ÷ 4 = **150 times** greater. (Quick method: the force is the same, so the pressure is 150 times greater because the area is 150 times smaller.) This is why thin heels can damage wooden floors.

blocks.title: Remember
items: pressure = force ÷ area; units Pa (N/m²) or N/cm². Small area → large pressure; large area → small pressure.
Gas pressure: moving particles collide with the walls. More particles, a higher temperature or a smaller volume → more collisions → more pressure.
Liquid pressure increases with depth and acts in all directions; liquids can hardly be compressed.
Diffusion: substances intermingle because their particles move randomly — fast in gases, slower in liquids, faster when hotter.
Particles never get bigger when heated — they move faster.
